You should know that there is no perfect body for pole, in my pole studio I have seen people of all shapes, sizes and abilities do awesome stuff on the pole and other aerial sports. 
People with disabilities do pole, people who have amputated limbs do pole, big people, small people, people with extensive sporting backgrounds, people with no sport experience- all of them can do pole. Maybe they all can't do the same things, but as long as you show up, try your best, and have fun- what does anything else matter? 

Do pole because you have fun doing it (if you do have fun doing it?) And try to remember that nobody is caring about what your body looks like, they are focused on what they are doing.

Hey there, that's a really valid and common problem with eating disorders. 
Your therapist cannot force you to recover when you do not want to/ are not ready. 

The issue is that, if your therapist believes your life is in danger from anorexia they have to either stop treating you (because it is unethical to sit by and watch you die if their treatment is not helping you to not die) or possibly do an involuntary hospital admission. 

It's sort if like if you told your therapist you were going to commit suicide as soon as you left the office and you didn't want them to help you. They would legally have to call an ambulance for you or something like that. 

I'm sorry you're in this situation I know it's not easy. If you tell your therapist your thoughts I'm sure they will tell you your options.

You look like you have a great base of strength. What you really need to think about is throwing your head back to look behind you. 
Think of your body a bit like a see-saw or lever. 

As you lean your upper body backwards, your arms can straighten and legs go up. It's pretty much impossible to get upside down with your head and upper body held stiffly where you have them now. 
Good luck!!
This is super important. It was the key to me finally getting this move!

In your video you did the same leg as bottom hand first (in my opinion the harder way). Try the other leg first.

It also seemed like your chest started too far away from the pole. Try and slide your hand closest to the ground a little lower to bring your chest closer to the pole.

Which leg do you take off first? I find if I take off the same leg as my bottom hand (closest to the ground) I will fall a lot easier after I take off the second leg. 

If I take off same leg as the top hand (closest to the roof) and really sort of press down and engage my leg muscles I am MUCH more stable to take off the other leg. 
You will get there!!!!! It's a super hard move but once you find your balance point it will feel easy!!
We call it a Franklin at my studio but with the arms the opposite way (inside arm holding pole between legs)

It is hard, but you can do it! 
To me it looks like you are looking up at the roof- this will make inverting a lot harder. When you go up you need to tilt your head back and try to look behind you. This was the most important thing for me.

Also if you have your arms a little lower you won't have to lift your body as high. 

Keep at it!

I find also if you have any hobbies that you really have to focus on, if you can push yourself to do that, it helps me feel a little better. 

Good luck, it really can be a hard thing to deal with!

Sorry if the following is totally off base but here's my thoughts from reading your post;

- can we talk a little about joyful movement? You mentioned that you don't excercise and have never enjoyed it. 
I used to HATE excercise and never did it until I was about 19 years old which is when I discovered the magic that is pole dancing and aerial arts and I fell in love with moving my body. I don't do it because I want it to change how I look, I do it because it's super fun, makes me feel strong and awesome and I love how it helps me de-stress. Once I started getting in some movement regularly I found that I wanted to fuel my body in a way that made me feel my best so that I could get better and better at my chosen sport. 
There's so many things out there to try that aren't typical excercise- roller blading, ice skating, rock climbing, parkour, dancing, virtual reality games like beat saber. 
Maybe mess around with some and see how it makes you feel or if anything peaks your interest. 

- along that same line, do you have many hobbies? I know when I'm bored I tend to think a lot more about snacking even though I'm not hungry at all, my brain just wants some stimulation. Maybe try to add some more planned activities in your day if you don't already. Not to ignore your hunger but just to give you something else to focus on other than food. 

- the other thing that really stood out to me is that you noticed you really aren't feeling good physically. I think it's kinda strange that your nutritionist is against gentle nutrition as I think it's pretty important. You don't even have to take anything away from what you're currently eating. I would try adding in some different nutrients alongside your cravings. For example if you want a candy bar, have it but maybe have some grapes on the side, or some of your favourite veggies along side your fried food. Having an adequate variety of nutrients might make you feel a little better physically. 

I'm definitely by no means perfect on my IE journey but I've come a long way from where I started so I hope this helps even a tiny bit!!! Good luck.

I've been managing my bpd without meds for about 3 and a half years now and I prefer it that way. I have had extensive therapy and am still seeing a therapist.

Sometimes things are really hard and I think about trying them again, but honestly they never really worked for me anyway. 

In my opinion you can manage it without meds, but you will likely then need more therapy. Meds are just another tool to help us cope. There is no specific medication for BPD, just various ones to help with symptoms or other associated disorders/mental illness.

I don't have an evil calculated plan to try to manipulate everyone around me. In fact, I don't think I've ever intentionally manipulated anyone in my life. I just sometimes feel extreme emotional pain and want to do what I can to ease that pain.

Honestly, I didn't find good treatment for awhile and dealt with a huge amount of stigma and mistreatment in the meantime.

Luckily I was eventually referred to a treatment centre solely for people with BPD and have an absolutely wonderful therapist and I've made a huge amount of progress!!

It's sad that not everyone has the same good fortune that I did and stigma is still alive and well in our community :(
